content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a denoising method for EEG timeseries (long, multi-channel scalp potential measurements) based on the Denoising Diffusion Probability Model, which itself is strongly related to Denoising Auto-encoders, and the multi-level Gaussian model of Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015. The authors propose the modelling of two separate noise sources, "Domain specific" noise and "Content specific" noise. The authors then introduce a classifier guidance module to encourage the "Domain specific" noise to be predictive of the subject index.

The authors fit the proposed two component noise model to EEG data, and provide correlational analyses.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
On page two (section 1 closing paragraphs) the authors talk about human artifact removal, which I assume to mean EEG signal specific to certain subjects but not general to a specific task. The authors claim that a two (or three) component model, one component that is subject specific, another that is "clean", and implicitly a noise component, is a widely accepted assumption. While a very high level this might be true, surely there are already numerous latent variable frameworks that model this explicitly. Instead, the authors have induced this separation using classifier guidance on the components of the DDPM.

I think overall that separating generating signal into two components is an interesting concept, and perhaps should be pursued further. However, having part of the noise be conditional on the DDPM leads to strange consequences in the original DDPM structure (iteratively applied layers of noising becomes...something else?), possibly changing the derived loss function. This remains unexplored in the current work.

I think the authors should think deeply about why they want to generate EEG data and what scientific question can be answered, and/or what piece of DDPM theory they would like to tackle by splitting the noise into separate components. Nine subjects with 3 seconds of EEG data at 250 Hz does not seem like a lot of data, even windowed at 75 step strides. How can we prove to ourselves that our model has learned anything meaningful here, aside from the dataset in front of it? I.e., how can we show any form of generalization. Is correlation with subjects in the training set valid?

It seems best conceptually to show extraction of "clean signal", but it is unclear how to do that in this framework. Must the DDPM be trained on each subject we wish to apply it to? This seems to be the case.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Occasionally standard notation and terminology is not kept, e.g., referring to the $\epsilon$ terms are referred to as variances.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper feels like the ad hoc application of DDPM to a new domain, with modification for subject-wise variance. There are some good conceptual beginnings here, but they feel underdeveloped, both from the theory side and the application side.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a DDPM based method for brain dynamics recognition. To deal with human-subject noise, the key idea is to represent a measured signal as a sum of clear signal and subject specific noise, which are orthogonal, and then plug this decomposition into DDPM, forming this so-called domain-specific DDPM.  Experiments are conducted to show that DS-DDPM alleviates subject-specific noise and improves EEG classification accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
The paper addresses a real challenge about how to deal with human-subject specific noise in EEG modeling.
The experimental results are competitive.

Weaknesses:
The proposed approach is straighforward and lacks core novelty (see below)
The paper contains quite some typos, grammatic errors, and mistakes in equation
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clairty: 
In general the paper is easy to follow but there are quite some typos and grammatic errors.
Also, there is a miss of $sqrt$ in Eq. (3) 

Novelty: 
The key idea of representing a measured signal as a sum of clear signal and subject specific noise, which are orthogonal, is not new. 
Plugging this decomposition into DDPM is rather straightforward and hence it is difficult to justify a high novelty solely based on this. 

Reproducibility: 
There is an open source code link provided.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the paper addresses a real challenge about how to deal with human-subject specific noise in EEG modeling and presents a reasonable DDPM-based approach for this. The results are competitives.
However the technical idea is rather straightforward and hence the novelty is below the ICLR standard. Plus there are quite some writing errors.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed domain-specific denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DS-DDPM) to remove human artifacts for EEG signals. They modeled artifact removal as a domain-specific denoising process and performed denoising by generating subject-specific domain variance and the invariant brain signals through the denoising process. In addition, downstream classification tasks further verify the effectiveness of the generated clean data. In general, it is well-written and organized.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. To remove the human artifacts, the authors introduced denoising diffusion probabilistic models for EEG signals, which benefit the downstream denoising and classification tasks.
2. The model was used to solve the actual problems in the real-world application, and domain-specific denoising could help improve the cross-subject EEG classification performance
3. Qualitative and quantitative results in the denoising and classification tasks task verify the effectiveness of the proposed DS-DDPM.

Weaknesses:
1. The overview of the framework (Fig. 3) is a little confusing.
2. The writing ability of the paper needs to be further improved. Some errors can be found in the paper. For example, on page 5, “which denotes the weights make the predictions only depend on the angle between the feature and the weight” lacks a period.
“we could formulate the Arc-Margin loss Larc coulde be defined in xx”, also had mistakes.
3. The paper lacks the statistical test that would make the results more reliable, for example in Figure 1 and Figure 2.
4. The authors should compare with the state-of-art EEG MI recognition models performed on the public EEG dataset since the final aim of the proposed model was for MI recognition.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is logically clear, detailed in description, relatively complete in experiments, and is a work of moderate quality.
content.summary_of_the_review: The innovation of this work is general. The proposed DS-DDPM model was first applied for EEG signals, aiming to denoise the EEG signals to get cleaned data and obtain the subject-specific and invariant representations. Considering the difficulty of EEG denoising, this work seems to be able to alleviate the problem of artifact removal and may have certain application prospects.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on the problem of EEG signal reconstruction under subject-specific variability, such that domain-invariant and subject-variant components of the input signals can be modeled by a generative denoising diffusion probabilistic model. In the reverse denoising process, signal separation is performed by exploiting subject-specific differences as domain variance (estimated with a supervised subject classifier), as well as an orthogonality constraint loss on the separately modeled latent outputs of the domain-variant and invariant processes. Proposed architecture, domain specific DDPMs (DS-DDPM), is evaluated on a BCI Competition IV motor imagery decoding dataset, in order to overcome domain distribution bias (i.e., subject variability) such that cross-subject decoding performance can be increased.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1) Proposed approach appears to be novel by its application with DDPMs. 
2) Another important strength is also the availability of visualizations for reconstructed signals, where the separated signals appear to maintain more than only the low-frequency components of the EEG inputs.

Weaknesses: 
1) Experimental evaluations are generally insufficient, as one should consistently demonstrate the benefit of the proposed approach on some other datasets (or even different BCI tasks). 
2) There is also no comparison to any recent methods tailored for cross-subject generalization in motor imagery decoding in the experiments, rather than a traditional ICA-based denoising approach. 
3) The language/writing needs improvements.
4) There are also some unclarified points regarding the algorithm's generative design perspective, while ultimately aiming to tackle an EEG-based decoding problem (please see detailed comments later).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty & Quality: The proposed approach on decomposing subject-variant and invariant components from EEG signals have been previously studied extensively, however the authors tackle this problem using DDPMs in a novel way. Experimental evaluations are rather weak and the quality of the manuscript is rather lower in that respect. 

Clarity: Overall methodological description is understandable. However the paper's language/narrative needs improvement. There are several grammatical fixes to be performed through the manuscript. Some examples that I can list from the Abstract: "The subjects differences in .." -> "Cross-subject differences",  "generalized ability" -> "generalization ability", "redesign the denoising process" -> "redesigning the denoising process", "normally considered subject-specific noises" -> "normally considered as subject-specific noises".

Reproducibility: Sufficient, since the authors provide their code/implementations.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I believe the methodology touches a very interesting problem with a relatively novel approach. However the validity of the proposal remains vague at this point and I have several concerns summarized below:
- Generally, experimental evaluations are shallow as they are restricted to only a single dataset. i.e., lacks comparisons to existing methods or evaluations on other motor imagery or BCI datasets. Regarding the current results in Table 2: The models are trained on a single subject and tested on several others. Can the authors demonstrate if their model is able to disentangle subject-specific information from multiple subjects at training time, and if successful, how this model generalizes to a left-out subject?
- There are several ambiguities regarding the UNet-EEG architecture as to why the architecture is simply chosen to be analogous to one from computer vision. There is no neurophysiological intuition provided on the choice of the temporal length of 224 time points while segmenting EEG. Given the signal sampling rate, why does the model end up using less than a second of EEG data in generative modeling of motor imagery EEG? How is this important (or not) to the design, can the authors discuss?
- No descriptions are provided regarding the diffusion model hyperparameters, e.g., sampling timesteps during training and inference? What was the noise distribution considered at time t=T for their model?
- No ablations on the loss regularizer hyperparameters are demonstrated/discussed. Should be performed.
- How consistent are the signal reconstructions (since the model is generative) and the resulting accuracies in Table 2?
- One general concern regarding the adopted methodology: Authors should clarify in their paper why does one need a generative modeling perspective at test time for a cross-subject classification problem? 
In a similar vein, there has been several previous work that have considered a similar subject-invariant representation learning approach by using an auxiliary subject-classifier, to separate domain-invariant and subject-variant components from EEG in a discriminative model [1]. Maybe the authors can discuss some intuitions on their perspective.
[1] "Learning invariant representations from EEG via adversarial inference." IEEE Access 2020.
- For reconstructed signals, it would be good to also include frequency domain visualizations (rather than only time-domain), such that one can perhaps clearly see high-frequency distortions being removed.
- Current version of the paper also misses to refer to the original [Ho et al. NeurIPS 2020] DDPM paper, on which the authors' work is basically based on.

content.title: Domain Specific Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models for Brain Dynamics
content.abstract: The distribution differences in brain dynamics according to different human subjects, which is a kind of human-subject noise, as referred to as human artifacts, have severely limited the generalized ability of brain dynamics recognition. Previous human artifact removal methods normally utilize traditional spectrum filtering or blind Source Separation techniques, based on a simple assumption of prior distributions, which limit the capacity of learning domain variance of each subject. We propose a new approach to model the removal of the human artifacts as a generative denoising process, which can generate and learn subject-specific domain variance and the invariant brain signals, simultaneously. We propose Domain Specific Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DS-DDPM) to decompose the denoising process into the subject domain variance and invariant content at each step. Subtle constraints and probabilistic design are proposed to formulate domain variance and invariant content into orthogonal spaces and further supervise the domain variance with the subject classifier. This method is the first work to explicitly separate human subject-specific variance through generative denoising processes, which outperforms previous methods in two aspects, 1) DS-DDPM could learn more accurate subject-specific domain variance by domain generative learning rather than previous filtering methods 2) DS-DDPM is the first work could explicitly generate subject noise distribution. Comprehensive experimental results suggest that DS-DDPM could help alleviate domain distribution bias for cross-domain brain dynamics signal recognition.
